topic: Octave-spaced sine waves under a fixed bell-shaped loudness curve make a pitch that seems to rise forever
summary: A Shepard tone sums sine waves an octave apart, fading the lowest and highest components. Moving all of them up together sounds like rising pitch, but after one octave the set is identical to where it started, so the rise never ends. Shepard used discrete steps; Jean-Claude Risset made a continuous glide. The effect rests on pitch having two parts, height and chroma, which can be drawn as a helix.

facts.claim: A Shepard tone is a superposition of sine waves separated by octaves; moved up or down together, it gives the illusion of a tone that continually rises or falls.
The Shepard scale uses discrete steps, while Jean-Claude Risset's version, the Shepard-Risset glissando, glides continuously.
Jean-Claude Risset was a French composer and pioneer of computer music.
Pitch circularity is a fixed sequence of tones that seems to rise or fall endlessly in pitch.
Shepard's helix of pitch places chroma around a cylinder and height along it, so octave-related pitches lie on one vertical line.
facts.source_title: Chroma and Shepard Tones, FMP Notebooks

facts.claim: Shepard tones are weighted superpositions of octave-separated sinusoids, with weights that fade out the lowest and highest components.
facts.source_title: Chroma and Shepard Tones, FMP Notebooks

facts.claim: In Diana Deutsch's tritone paradox, the same pair of Shepard tones a half-octave apart is heard as rising by some listeners and as falling by others.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Octave-spaced partial hand-off
visualisable_mechanisms.description: All partials rise together; the top one fades out as a new one fades in at the bottom, so after one octave the sound is unchanged.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Show partials as beads riding a spiral outward, fading at the rim and appearing at the centre.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Gaussian spectral envelope
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A fixed bell over log-frequency sets each partial's loudness, so the overall spectral centre never moves.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Draw the bell as a glowing ring and a ribbon with each partial's level.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Chroma helix
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Pitch has height and chroma; seen from above, the helix becomes a log spiral where octaves line up on one ray.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Use a log spiral with one turn per octave, so turning it one full turn equals zooming by two.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Discrete scale versus glide
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Shepard's original steps a semitone at a time; Risset's version glides.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Start with twelve semitone steps, then switch to a continuous glide.

open_questions: How wide can the loudness bell get before listeners hear the top partial leave?
Does the illusion survive if the partials are not exactly an octave apart?

surprise.justification: Many people have heard the endless rise, but few know it is just a handful of octave-spaced sines under a fixed loudness bell.
